input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-320: Principles of Data Management. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides a broad introduction to the principles and practice of modern data management, with an emphasis on the relational database model. Topics in relational database systems include data modeling; the relational model; relational algebra; Structured Query Language (SQL); and data quality, transactions, integrity and security. Students will also learn approaches to building relational database application programs. Additional topics include object-oriented and object-relational databases; semi-structured databases (such as XML); and information retrieval. A database project is required. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-320]
This course provides a broad introduction to the principles and practice of modern data management, with an emphasis on the relational database model. Topics in relational database systems include data modeling; the relational model; relational algebra; Structured Query Language (SQL); and data quality, transactions, integrity and security. Students will also learn approaches to building relational database application programs. Additional topics include object-oriented and object-relational databases; semi-structured databases (such as XML); and information retrieval. A database project is required. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-142 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-124 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Modern data management focuses on organizing, storing, and retrieving information efficiently using structured models.
beats.example: A hospital system uses a relational database to link patient records, medical history, and appointment schedules.
beats.title: Introduction to Data Management
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple flowchart showing data flowing from collection to structured storage and retrieval.

beats.claim: The relational model organizes data into tables with rows and columns, where each column represents an attribute and each row represents a record.
beats.example: An 'Employees' table contains columns for EmployeeID, Name, Department, and Salary.
beats.title: Relational Model Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Show a basic table layout with labeled rows and columns, highlighting the entity-attribute relationship.

beats.claim: Data modeling involves defining entities, attributes, and relationships to accurately represent real-world scenarios in a database.
beats.example: A 'Student' entity relates to a 'Course' entity through an 'Enrollment' relationship, linking student IDs to course codes.
beats.title: Data Modeling Concepts
beats.visualDirection: Draw a simple ER diagram with Student, Course, and Enrollment boxes and lines connecting them.

beats.claim: Relational algebra provides a set of operations to manipulate relational data, such as selection, projection, and join.
beats.example: A selection operation filters the 'Employees' table to show only those in the 'Engineering' department.
beats.title: Relational Algebra Basics
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a before-and-after table showing rows filtered by a condition using selection notation.

beats.claim: SQL is a standard language used to query, update, and manage relational databases through declarative statements.
beats.example: The command SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Department = 'Marketing' retrieves specific records.
beats.title: Structured Query Language (SQL)
beats.visualDirection: Display a code snippet of the SQL query alongside the resulting filtered table output.

beats.claim: Data quality ensures information is accurate, complete, consistent, and timely to support reliable decision-making.
beats.example: Validating that all 'PhoneNumber' fields follow a standard format prevents duplicate or corrupted contact records.
beats.title: Data Quality Principles
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with icons for accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness.

beats.claim: Transaction integrity maintains database consistency through atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID) properties.
beats.example: A banking transaction updates both account balances atomically, ensuring neither account is left in an inconsistent state.
beats.title: Transaction Integrity
beats.visualDirection: Create a step-by-step diagram showing a transaction process with ACID checkpoints at each stage.

beats.claim: Database security protects data through encryption, access controls, and authentication to prevent unauthorized access.
beats.example: Role-based access control limits 'view' permissions to analysts while restricting 'delete' permissions to administrators.
beats.title: Database Security Practices
beats.visualDirection: Display a permission matrix table showing user roles and their corresponding database actions.

beats.claim: Building relational database application programs involves integrating SQL queries with application logic to automate data workflows.
beats.example: An e-commerce platform uses SQL to fetch product inventory and application code to process checkout orders.
beats.title: Application Development Approaches
beats.visualDirection: Sketch a simple architecture diagram with a frontend app, backend logic, and relational database connected by SQL calls.

beats.claim: Evaluating a relational database system requires verifying data modeling accuracy, SQL query efficiency, integrity constraints, and security configurations.
beats.example: A developer checks that foreign keys enforce referential integrity, indexes optimize query performance, and encryption protects sensitive fields.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a printable checklist graphic with checkboxes for modeling, querying, integrity, and security verification.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of the relational database model, including entities, attributes, and relationships.
Explain how Structured Query Language (SQL) is used to retrieve, update, and manage relational data.
Apply data quality, transaction integrity, and security principles to design a secure relational database system.
